recipes.title: Active users & event volume over time (DAU/WAU/MAU)
recipes.when_to_use: How many unique users / events over time, at day/week/month grain.
recipes.notes: DAU/MAU ratio (stickiness) = active_users at day vs month grain.
recipes.hack: count_distinct of the entity key = unique actors; group_by {time: metric_time, grain} turns any measure into a time series. Extrapolate: unique-X-over-time = count_distinct(entity) scoped to the X event.

recipes.title: Metric sliced by a user attribute
recipes.when_to_use: Revenue / payers / ARPPU broken down by country, platform, media_source, acquisition_type or campaign_id.
recipes.notes: User attributes via the implicit events.user -> users.user join; campaign_id is a plain string attribute on dim_users (1-hop, like country/platform) — there is no separate campaigns table.
recipes.hack: Any measure + group_by { model: 'users', attribute: '<attr>' } makes the semantic layer join the user dimension — no join written. Extrapolate: segment ANY metric by ANY user attribute the same way.

recipes.title: 2-step conversion funnel (level_started -> level_completed)
recipes.when_to_use: Step conversion / completion rate between two events within a window.
recipes.notes: Conversion base/conversion measures must be count_distinct. No native N-step funnel; chain 2-step conversions or use derived over step counts.
recipes.hack: A funnel step = an event narrowed by an event_data property value, counted as count_distinct(user); step conversion = ratio(next_step / prev_step). Extrapolate to any 2-step drop-off.

recipes.title: Multi-step funnel where each step = event + property value
recipes.when_to_use: Onboarding/activation funnels whose steps are the SAME event with a different property value (e.g. tutorial element_of_event_data=step_1 -> step_2 -> step_3), with step-to-step conversion.
recipes.notes: A funnel step is a measure scoped by event_name + a property `where` (event_data value). Steps chain as 2-step conversion metrics (s1->s2, s2->s3); multiply/compose for end-to-end. IMPORTANT: the step VALUES here (step_1..step_3) are an example — discover the real step values of your data first via semantic_index({ source, property: 'element_of_event_data' }) and substitute them. Could also key the step on level_id, screen_to, placement, etc.
recipes.hack: Chain one count_distinct(user) measure per step (event + property value) and ratio metrics between consecutive steps. Extrapolate to any ordered N-step sequence.

recipes.title: N-day retention (D1/D7) via conversion window
recipes.when_to_use: Share of newly-acquired users who return (start a session) within N days of first launch.
recipes.notes: Cohort = users with a first_launch (acquisition); returned = users who start a new_session within the window. base_measure and conversion_measure are DIFFERENT events so the rate is meaningful (not identically 1.0). Approximates N-day retention via conversion window; exact point-in-time D-N retention is not expressible as a governed metric.
recipes.hack: Retention = a conversion metric (base = first/install event, conversion = a later activity event) with window = 'N day'. Extrapolate: change N or the base/return events for any Dn.

recipes.title: Acquisition-cohort grid (install date x activity)
recipes.when_to_use: Cohort table: metric by install_date cohort and activity day.
recipes.notes: Group by install_date (cohort) and metric_time (age). Cumulative LTV per cohort can layer a cumulative metric.
recipes.hack: Pivot a retention measure by install-cohort (a time dimension) against age-in-days. Extrapolate: any cohort-attribute × age-bucket grid.

recipes.title: Behavioral cohort: users who did / didn't do event X
recipes.when_to_use: Segment users by whether they performed a behavior (e.g. purchased), then compare metrics.
recipes.notes: Split did/didn't with a Metric() in --where, e.g. `{{ Metric('behavior_purchases', group_by=['user']) }} > 0`.
recipes.hack: Split the population by a behavioral flag (did event X) then measure later behavior on each arm. Extrapolate to any 'did A → compare B' cohort.

recipes.title: Visit-to-purchase conversion (native conversion metric)
recipes.when_to_use: Share of visitors who purchase within a window.
recipes.notes: Use constant_properties to require the same product across base/conversion events when relevant.
recipes.hack: conversion metric linking two events by the shared user entity (base=visit, conversion=purchase). Extrapolate to any A→B funnel within a window.

recipes.title: Level progression: completion, attempts, time per level
recipes.when_to_use: Per-level difficulty: starts, completes, completion rate, avg time/attempts.
recipes.notes: Group by the JSON-extracted level_id dimension. Churn-at-level derived from starts of level N vs N+1 in post-processing.
recipes.hack: Group an event measure by a numeric event_data ordinal (level_id) and ratio adjacent values = progression/drop-off. Extrapolate to any per-step numeric progression.

recipes.title: Monetization: revenue, ARPPU, AOV, by product/channel/day
recipes.when_to_use: IAP revenue, payers, ARPPU, average order value over time and by segment/product.
recipes.notes: LTV curve = cumulative revenue over metric_time by acquisition cohort (needs time spine).
recipes.hack: Per-X average = a value measure ÷ a population measure via a ratio metric (revenue ÷ users = ARPU; ÷ payers = ARPPU). Extrapolate: any 'total per entity' = ratio(sum, count_distinct).

recipes.title: Ad monetization: ad revenue & impressions by network/placement
recipes.when_to_use: Ad revenue, impressions, eCPM-style splits by ad_network/placement/ad_type.
recipes.notes: Ad revenue lives on ad_finished.revenue. eCPM = rev_per_imp * 1000 (post-process).
recipes.hack: Aggregate a value property (revenue) grouped by its categorical context properties (network/format/placement). Extrapolate: sum(value) by its descriptor dimensions for any breakdown.

recipes.title: In-game economy: coin sources vs sinks
recipes.when_to_use: Coins earned (income) vs spent (outcome) by source/placement.
recipes.notes: net_coins is a derived metric (income - outcome). Source/sink breakdown via source_type.
recipes.hack: Two oppositely-scoped sum measures + a derived expr (in − out) = net flow / balance. Extrapolate to any signed two-sided quantity (faucets vs sinks, credits vs debits).

recipes.title: Stickiness (DAU/MAU) & active base over time
recipes.when_to_use: How sticky the product is and how the active base evolves.
recipes.notes: DAU/MAU ratio = active_users at day grain / active_users at month grain.
recipes.hack: Query the SAME count_distinct measure at two grains (day vs month) and divide = stickiness. Extrapolate: ratio of one measure across two windows.

recipes.title: A/B test — conversion rate by variant (with significance)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a conversion rate (e.g. purchase) between experiment variants and test whether the difference is significant.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows are n + conversions per variant (exposed = users with in-window events). Then call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: proportion }): control = the control variant_group row, variants = the rest. For a continuous metric (revenue/ARPU per user), aggregate per-user then per-variant mean+stddev and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }).
recipes.hack: Join the experiments source, window events to [assigned_at, ended_at], flag conversion per user (compute case → aggregate max), then aggregate n + conversions per variant and call experiment({ action: 'analyze' }). Extrapolate: per-variant rate (proportion) or per-user mean+stddev (Welch) for ANY experiment metric.

recipes.title: Cumulative & period-to-date revenue (running totals)
recipes.when_to_use: Running total of revenue over time, and month-to-date (resets each month). Showcases the cumulative metric type.
recipes.notes: cumulative with no window = running total from the start; grain_to_date:month = month-to-date (resets monthly). Add `window` (e.g. "7 day") for a trailing rolling-window cumulative.
recipes.hack: cumulative metric over a sum measure = running total; grain_to_date resets each period (MTD/WTD); add a window for a trailing rolling total. Extrapolate to any accumulating quantity over time.

recipes.title: Blended revenue (IAP + ads) via a derived metric
recipes.when_to_use: Combine two revenue streams (IAP in USD + ad revenue in cents) into one blended metric. Showcases the derived metric type.
recipes.notes: derived metric = arithmetic over other metrics; here ad revenue (cents) is converted to USD (/100) and added to IAP USD. Only metric names, numbers and + - * / ( ) are allowed in expr.
recipes.hack: derived metric = a formula over other metrics (incl. unit conversion like /100). Extrapolate: blend/normalize/combine any set of metrics into one composite number.

recipes.title: A/B test — revenue per user by variant (Welch t-test)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a CONTINUOUS metric (revenue/ARPU/time per user) between experiment variants and test significance.
recipes.hack: Per-user continuous A/B: window events to the assignment period, coalesce the per-event value to 0, sum per user (one value per exposed user), then per variant compute n + avg + stddev and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }) (Welch). Extrapolate to ANY per-user continuous metric (revenue, session time, items) between variants.
recipes.notes: mean A/B needs per-variant n, mean and stddev of a PER-USER value (aggregate per user first, then per variant). experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }) runs Welch t-test: control = control variant_group row, variants = the rest.

recipes.title: A/B test — CUPED variance reduction (pre-experiment covariate)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a continuous metric between variants with MORE POWER by adjusting for each user's pre-experiment value of the same metric (CUPED).
recipes.hack: CUPED = variance reduction via a pre-experiment covariate: per user compute Y (metric inside [assigned_at, ended_at]) and X (same metric BEFORE assigned_at) with two compute-case windows, then per variant emit the sufficient sums n, ΣY, ΣY², ΣX, ΣX², ΣXY (sum of Y, Y*Y, X, X*X, X*Y) and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: cuped }). Extrapolate: any continuous A/B gains power when a correlated pre-period covariate exists — no per-user data leaves SQL, only the 6 sums.
recipes.notes: CUPED needs a PRE-experiment covariate (the same metric before assignment); it removes its variance, raising power, and reduces to a plain t-test when there is no pre-period signal. Pass per-variant sufficient sums; the tool computes the pooled theta and runs Welch on the adjusted means.

recipes.title: A/B test — ratio metric via the delta method (e.g. level completion rate)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a RATIO metric between variants where the unit of analysis is finer than the randomization unit — e.g. levels completed per level started, or clicks per impression, when users (not attempts) are randomized.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows carry, per variant: n (users) plus the per-user numerator/denominator sums and their squares/cross-product. Then call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: ratio }): control = the control variant_group row, variants = the rest. The ratio is Σnumerator/Σdenominator; the delta method turns the per-user sums into a cluster-robust variance, so attempts within a user are not treated as independent.
recipes.hack: For a ratio metric whose denominator is counted at a finer grain than the randomization unit (events/sessions per user), aggregate numerator & denominator PER USER first so each user is one independent observation, then carry forward their squares (num², den²) and cross-product (num·den) and sum per variant. experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: ratio }) applies the delta method for the correct (cluster-robust) variance — a plain proportion test on pooled events would understate it. Extrapolate to CTR (clicks/impressions), completion rate, ARPDAU, etc.

recipes.title: A/B guardrail — Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) check
recipes.when_to_use: BEFORE trusting any lift: verify the observed per-variant split matches the intended one. A mismatch means randomization or logging is broken and the whole experiment is invalid.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows are the number of EXPOSED users per variant (distinct users with in-window events). Feed those counts to experiment({ action: 'check_split' }): it runs a χ² goodness-of-fit against the intended split (equal by default; pass expected_ratio for an uneven design). p < 0.001 ⇒ srm_detected=true ⇒ STOP and fix assignment/logging before reading any metric. This is a guardrail, not a metric — run it alongside the metric recipes (conversion/revenue/ratio/cuped).
recipes.hack: Count distinct exposed users per variant in the warehouse, then compare observed vs intended counts with experiment({ action: 'check_split' }) (χ² goodness-of-fit). Extrapolate: ANY 'observed category counts vs an expected split' sanity check (traffic allocation, platform mix, day-of-week balance) is the same χ² test.

recipes.title: A/B planning — sample size & minimum detectable effect (power)
recipes.when_to_use: BEFORE launching, to size the test (how many users per variant to detect a target effect), or given the traffic you have, to find the smallest effect you can detect (MDE). Also AFTER an inconclusive test, to tell 'no effect' apart from 'underpowered'.
recipes.notes: experiment({ action: 'plan' }) is a pure calculation (no warehouse). Provide a baseline rate (metric=proportion) or a stddev (metric=mean) plus EXACTLY ONE of mde (→ required n per group) or n (→ minimum detectable effect). Estimate the baseline/stddev from a monetization_metrics or active_users_trend query first, then plan. Pair every experiment({ action: 'analyze' }) with an up-front MDE so a non-significant result can be read correctly.
recipes.hack: Up-front power analysis: baseline/stddev + target effect → required n per group; or n → MDE. Run it before the test to size it and after an inconclusive test to check it was powered. Extrapolate to any two-arm comparison (proportion z-test or mean t-test).

recipes.title: D1/D7 retention split by a user attribute (country / platform / source)
recipes.when_to_use: Diagnose a retention change: which segment (country, platform, media_source, acquisition_type) drives the drop or growth in D1/D7 retention.
recipes.notes: Same conversion-window construction as nday_retention, plus use_base_models:['users'] so the user attributes are JOINABLE: group_by { model: 'users', attribute: '<attr>' }. Compare segments side by side to localize a retention change before investigating causes.
recipes.hack: ANY metric becomes a per-segment diagnostic by adding use_base_models:['users'] + group_by { model: 'users', attribute: '<attr>' }. Localize first (which segment moved), then drill into that segment.

recipes.title: Exact day-N retention curve (returned ON day N, not within N days)
recipes.when_to_use: Classic game-analytics retention curve: for each day-offset N since install, how many users were active exactly on that day. Use when 'within N days' (nday_retention) is not strict enough.
recipes.notes: day_n = date_diff(install_date -> device_time) buckets every session by its exact day offset since install; returners at day_n=N over the cohort size = exact D-N retention. Divide by the cohort (day_n=0 row, or a separate first_launch count) to get rates. This is point-in-time retention — stricter than the conversion-window approximation in nday_retention. The join uses the declared 'user' relationship, so it needs no column names. If the install record is SLOWLY-CHANGING (semantic_index({ model }) shows a validity window), add between: { value: 'device_time', from: '<validity start>', to: '<validity end>' } to the join stage — otherwise every session matches every historical version of the player and the returner counts inflate.
recipes.hack: Exact Dn = join the install date, date_diff it against the activity time, group by the offset. The same offset axis powers cohort heatmaps and lifetime curves.

recipes.title: Sessionization: rebuild sessions from raw events by inactivity gap
recipes.when_to_use: Session metrics (length, depth, events-per-session) when you cannot trust a client session counter — rebuild sessions server-side as bursts of activity separated by an inactivity gap (30 min here).
recipes.notes: lag() gives the previous event time per user; a NULL or >30min gap starts a new session; the running sum of session starts assigns a session index; aggregating by (user, session_idx) yields one row per rebuilt session with depth and duration. Tune the 1800s threshold to your product.
recipes.hack: Gap-based sessionization = lag -> gap -> CASE flag -> running-sum id -> aggregate. The same flag+running-sum pattern builds ANY 'episode' grouping (streaks, visits, bouts).

recipes.title: Period-over-period comparison (revenue by day with delta vs previous period)
recipes.when_to_use: WoW/DoD/MoM readouts: a metric per period plus its change vs the previous period, in one result.
recipes.notes: lag(revenue) over the period axis gives the previous period in the same row; delta/pct_change follow with plain arithmetic. CAVEAT: lag is the previous ROW — if periods can be missing (days with zero revenue), densify the axis first or compare at a coarser grain (week/month via date_trunc granularity).
recipes.hack: Period-over-period = aggregate to the period grain, then window lag + sub/div. Swap the measure or the grain freely; the same lag pattern yields growth rates and streak detection.

recipes.title: Data-quality check: event volume + distinct users per event
recipes.when_to_use: FIRST move when a metric looks anomalous: did the underlying events change volume (tracking broke, release dropped an event) or did real behavior change? Also a fast map of which events dominate the data.
recipes.notes: Compare volumes and per-event user counts against expectation/history; a vanished or collapsed event usually means broken tracking, not changed behavior. Drill NULL coverage of a suspicious property with semantic_index({ source, property }) — it separates expected NULLs (property not applicable to the event) from real gaps. Add a time_range to audit a specific release window, or group_by a user attribute (join 'users') to localize a client-side break.
recipes.hack: Anomaly triage order: (1) event volumes, (2) property NULL coverage, (3) only then the metric itself. Most 'metric drops' are tracking changes.

recipes.title: Two-sample significance for ANY two groups (no experiment needed)
recipes.when_to_use: You have TWO groups from the SAME pipeline and want to know if a difference is statistically real — NOT a randomized experiment. E.g. mean time-to-first vs time-to-last occurrence, conversion of cohort A vs B, a metric before vs after a date, organic vs paid. There is NO experiments-assignment table involved.
recipes.notes: Don't hand-roll a t-test/z-test. Compute per-group aggregates with a build_native_model pipeline, then feed them to ab_test — 'control'/'variants' are just group A vs group B(…). For a CONTINUOUS metric (time, value, count per unit): aggregate per group to n + mean (avg) + stddev, then ab_test({ metric: 'mean' }) (Welch t-test). For a RATE: aggregate to conversions + n per group, then ab_test({ metric: 'proportion' }) (two-proportion z-test). The pipeline that produces the groups can be ANY grouping — a CASE/derive column, two event_data values, a date split — it does NOT require the experiments role. The tool_calls below show the final ab_test step on example per-group aggregates.
recipes.hack: Compare two groups → aggregate each to its sufficient stats (mean: n+mean+stddev; proportion: conversions+n) in one pipeline, then ONE ab_test call returns lift + p-value + CI + significance. Reuse for first-vs-last, before-vs-after, cohort-vs-cohort — anywhere you'd otherwise eyeball two numbers.

recipes.title: A value from a lookup — merge, never map
recipes.when_to_use: You have a mapping (id → label, day → target, country → tier) and want it as a column.
recipes.approach: Put the other side in a frame and MERGE on the key: `lookup = bpd.DataFrame({"k": [...], "v": [...]}); df = df.merge(lookup, on="k", how="left")`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["v"] = df["k"].map(mapping)` — map aligns two objects by index, and the frame from dbt.ref() has none: NullIndexError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: The dict keys must have the SAME type as the column they join on — bpd.DataFrame turns Python strings into STRING, so a numeric key needs numbers, not "1". how="left" keeps unmatched rows with NULL; how="inner" drops them, which is a different question.
recipes.hack: Any "value from somewhere else" is a merge: a dict, a groupby result, a second table, a threshold per group. Build the other side as a frame with the key as a COLUMN, then merge.

recipes.title: A group's aggregate back on its rows — transform or merge
recipes.when_to_use: Share of a group's total, deviation from a group mean, "how big is my cohort" as a column.
recipes.approach: Same number of rows → `df["m"] = df.groupby("k")["x"].transform("mean")` (broadcasts inside ONE frame). A different shape, or several aggregates → build it with `groupby(..., as_index=False)` and MERGE it back.
recipes.instead_of: `df["m"] = df.groupby("k")["x"].mean()` — the groupby result is another object with its own index; assigning it needs alignment the frame cannot do.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: as_index=False keeps the key as a COLUMN — without it the key becomes the index and there is nothing to merge on. rename() before the merge, or both sides bring a column of the same name and the merge suffixes them.
recipes.hack: Two forms, one rule: inside one frame — transform; between two frames — merge. Never assignment.

recipes.title: Distinct values — a groupby, not unique()
recipes.when_to_use: A distinct list of ids, of (user, level) pairs, of values a column takes.
recipes.approach: `uniq = df.groupby(["k"], as_index=False).size().drop(columns="size")` — the documented replacement for this runtime.
recipes.instead_of: `df["k"].unique()` / `df.drop_duplicates(subset=["k"])` — both are unsupported in partial ordering mode.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: size() is what makes it a groupby rather than an aggregate over a column — drop it afterwards, or keep it and you have the counts for free. In a SQL stage the same thing is an aggregate with no measures; prefer that when you are not already in python.
recipes.hack: De-duplication is a GROUPING, not a row operation: group by the columns that define uniqueness, keep one row per group.

recipes.title: Top-N and anything positional — sort_values first
recipes.when_to_use: Top/bottom N, "the largest", "the first row per group", anything positional.
recipes.approach: `top = df.sort_values("x", ascending=False).head(10)` — or `df.nlargest(10, "x")`, which orders by itself.
recipes.instead_of: `df.head(10)` on an unsorted frame (its rows differ between runs) and `df.iloc[:10]` (raises OrderRequiredError).
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: This frame has no row order of its own, so "the first N" is only defined after a sort. For a quick LOOK at the data during development use peek(n) instead — it returns an arbitrary sample and is the cheaper call.
recipes.hack: Order is data: state it (sort_values / nlargest) wherever the answer depends on it, and never rely on the order rows happen to arrive in.

recipes.title: Rolling / shift / cumulative — sort, then the operation
recipes.when_to_use: 7-day averages, day-over-day deltas, cumulative totals, previous-value comparisons.
recipes.approach: `df = df.sort_values(order_key)` and then the series operation: `rolling(window=n).mean()`, `shift(1)`, `cumsum()`, `diff()`, `pct_change()`.
recipes.instead_of: Calling rolling/shift/cumsum on the frame as it arrives — the window is then over an arbitrary order, and the numbers are silently meaningless.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: Aggregate to the grain of the series FIRST (one row per day here) — rolling over raw events is both wrong and expensive. The first window-1 rows come back NULL by definition: say so, or drop them in a following SQL stage.
recipes.hack: Order-dependent operations are a pair: sort_values on the axis, then the operation. One sort is enough for the whole function.

recipes.title: A statistic OF the frame back ON it — a broadcast scalar
recipes.when_to_use: z-score, share of total, distance from the mean, normalisation.
recipes.approach: An aggregate OF the frame applied back TO it: `df["z"] = (df["x"] - df["x"].mean()) / df["x"].std(ddof=0)`; `df["share"] = df["x"] / df["x"].sum()`.
recipes.instead_of: Computing the statistic in one frame and joining it in from another — unnecessary here, and it needs an index.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: mean()/sum()/std() of the SAME frame come back as scalars and broadcast over its rows — one statement, no alignment. ddof=0 is the population deviation, ddof=1 the sample one; say which you used when reporting a z-score.
recipes.hack: Whole-frame statistic → scalar → column. Safe for mean, sum, std, min, max, count and a single quantile.

recipes.title: A threshold from the distribution — one quantile as a scalar
recipes.when_to_use: "The slowest 10%", "unusually hard levels", any "above normal" where nobody has defined normal.
recipes.approach: `cut = df["x"].quantile(0.9)` (a SCALAR) → write it as a column and compare: `df["p90"] = cut; df["is_high"] = df["x"] >= cut`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["x"].quantile([0.5, 0.9])` — a SERIES indexed by q, which this runtime has no index to align; and a hard-coded threshold nobody can defend.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: Ask for ONE q at a time. Several quantiles at once belong in a SQL stage (aggregate with fn=percentile), which returns them as columns instead of an indexed series. Keeping the threshold as a column makes the cut visible in the result instead of hidden in a filter.
recipes.hack: A cut-off computed FROM the data (median, p90, IQR) written back as a column, then compared row by row.

recipes.title: Filtering by another frame's data — merge the flag in
recipes.when_to_use: Keeping only qualifying users, excluding a blacklist, filtering by a per-group condition.
recipes.approach: Merge the other side in and filter on the merged column: `df = df.merge(flags, on="k", how="inner")` (or how="left" then `df[df["flag"]]`).
recipes.instead_of: `df[other["flag"]]` / `df[df["k"].isin(other_series)]` — a Series from ANOTHER frame has no index to align with this one.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: A mask built from the SAME frame (df[df["x"] > 0]) is always fine — this rule is only about a condition that lives in another object. An inner merge on the key IS the semi-join SQL would run; dropping the helper column keeps the output clean.
recipes.hack: "Keep the rows that are in X" = build X as a frame of keys and inner-merge it. Same move for "exclude": merge with how="left" and keep the NULLs.

recipes.title: An ml prediction back as a column (bigframes.ml)
recipes.when_to_use: Clustering, scoring, classification, a predicted value per row.
recipes.approach: Fit and predict INSIDE BigQuery, then take the prediction column off the result: `model.fit(X); df["segment"] = model.predict(X)["CENTROID_ID"]`. Scale first when the algorithm is distance-based.
recipes.instead_of: sklearn / scipy — they need `to_pandas()` first and then run single-node in the notebook; and a per-row Python scoring function, which this runtime cannot execute.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: predict() returns BigQuery ML's own columns — CENTROID_ID for clustering, predicted_<label> for a supervised model — which is why it is subscripted. The prediction is a column of the SAME frame, so nothing needs aligning. A SQL stage after it profiles the groups: the segment number alone answers nothing.
recipes.hack: Feature table in SQL → fit/predict in one python stage → prediction as a column → profile in SQL. The shape holds for every estimator; only the class and the output column change.

recipes.title: An estimator whose output REPLACES the frame — declare its columns
recipes.when_to_use: Forecasting, model metrics, a transformed matrix — anything where the result is not "my rows plus a column".
recipes.approach: When the estimator returns its OWN shape (forecast, score, metrics), the python stage returns THAT frame and `output.columns` describes it: `out = model.predict(horizon=30); return out`.
recipes.instead_of: Declaring the input columns as the output — the following SQL stages then reference columns that do not exist.

History IS the input: one row per period, no gaps. One model per series — a per-segment forecast is one model per segment, not one call.
recipes.hack: Whenever an estimator's output is its own table (forecast, score, metrics, transform), the stage's output.columns describes THAT table — and the SQL after it works on those names.

recipes.title: An expensive intermediate read twice — cache()
recipes.when_to_use: One heavy join or aggregate feeding several outputs in the same function.
recipes.approach: Materialize it once: `joined = df.merge(other, on="k"); joined.cache()` and derive everything from `joined`.
recipes.instead_of: Deriving several results from the same expensive expression without caching — execution is deferred, so each dependent result re-runs the whole thing.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: cache() writes a temporary BigQuery table — you pay for its storage, so use it for an intermediate that is genuinely read more than once (a join, a heavy groupby), not for every line. It is a hint about REUSE, not a speed-up of a single pass.
recipes.hack: Deferred execution means "written once" is not "computed once". If two or more results read the same intermediate, cache it.

recipes.title: What only SQL can do — bigframes.bigquery (bbq)
recipes.when_to_use: LEAST/GREATEST, array aggregation, building a STRUCT column, epoch conversions, a SQL function with no pandas name.
recipes.approach: Reach the BigQuery function directly: `bbq.sql_scalar("LEAST({0}, {1})", columns=[df["a"], df["b"]])`, `bbq.array_agg(df.groupby("k")["c"])`, `bbq.struct(df[["a","b"]])`, `bbq.unix_micros(df["t"])`.
recipes.instead_of: `to_pandas()` to get a Python equivalent — that leaves BigQuery and brings the whole result into the notebook.

recipes.notes: sql_scalar takes a single-column expression with {0}, {1} … placeholders bound to the columns you pass — it is not a place for a whole query. Everything in bbq still compiles to SQL and runs in BigQuery.
recipes.hack: Before converting to pandas for a missing function, look in bbq: arrays, structs, epochs and an arbitrary scalar SQL expression are all there.

recipes.title: Leaving for pandas only after the aggregation
recipes.when_to_use: A library call that only exists in pandas/numpy, on a small aggregated result.
recipes.approach: Aggregate in the warehouse FIRST, convert the small result: `small = df.groupby("k", as_index=False)["x"].sum(); pdf = small.to_pandas()`.
recipes.instead_of: `pdf = df.to_pandas()` on the incoming frame — it downloads the whole table into the notebook runtime and everything after it is single-node.

recipes.notes: The model must return a frame this runtime can materialize, so a pandas result goes back with bpd.read_pandas(). Do this only when the operation genuinely has no frame equivalent — and only on an already-aggregated table, because the download and everything after it happen on one node.
recipes.hack: The boundary is a decision, not a convenience: aggregate, then convert, then convert back. If the frame you hand to to_pandas() could be large, the approach is wrong.
